newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Industry says governments must help it go green.
newsitem.headline: Industry says governments must help it go green.

text.p: There will be little incentive for the electricity industry to promote less polluting ways of generating and using energy until governments provide the right policy framework, senior industry officials said on Wednesday.
"You can't get industry to invest in something that is not cost-effective," Andreas Papageorgi, the energy and economics chief of Britain's National Grid Group, told Reuters.

Electricity companies were seeking to earn more money by cutting costs but they could not do this by using renewable sources like wind and solar power or by switching from selling kilowatt hours to selling energy services like efficient boilers, insulation and double glazing, Papageorgi said.

He was speaking in the margins of a conference organised by the European Commission and the European electricity grouping Eurelectric to discuss how the electricity sector could contribute to environmentally and economically sustainable development.

It comes as European Union countries are trying to forge a common front to present to an international climate change summit in Kyoto, Japan, in December, where some 150 nations will aim to agree on legally binding targets to cut greenhouse gases.

According to British university professor John Chesshire, whose report on sustainable energy policies was the focus of the conference, the electricity sector consumes a third of Europe's primary fuel and is an obvious target for environmental concern because its generates CO2 and other gases which produce global warming, noise, eyesores and in some cases nuclear waste.

Eurelectric president Niek Ketting told a news conference the industry was aware of the pressing need for action, which includes increasing the percentage of renewables used to generate electricity and encouraging customers to buy from the utilities less electricity and more energy-saving services.

Ketting said the industry needed the support of Brussels and governments but its first move after the conference would not be until the autumn, when it plans to hold talks with Commission environment and energy officials on a plan of action.
Once competition is introduced into the European electricity market, the utilities will be engaged in a mad scramble to keep customers, firstly through cutting prices, Papageorgi said.

He said he agreed with Dutch industry minister Hans Wijers who told the news conference the industry would only seriously start trying to sell green electricity to customers if governments increased the price of fossil fuels through taxes, thus making relatively expensive renewables more competitive.

Only when there was no more leeway for competing on price would the utilites turn to selling packages of energy services -- finding ways to cut customers' fuel bills in return for a five- to seven-year contract to buy electricity from a particular supplier -- Papageorgi said.
And once the customer's contract with the service provider ended, the supplier would be back in the price war to keep that consumer, he added.
